title: Parenting as practice
hookLine: parenthood as practice: the Buddha's son asks for his inheritance, and a grandfather's grief becomes a rule
tomorrow: a poet woke up lost in a dark wood. who came to find him?

lines: A BIG CALLING, AND A KID.
cards: An argument that turns up in comment sections: can you follow a big calling and still be a good mom or dad? Buddhists have their own version, and it starts with a little boy.

Tradition says the Buddha left home soon after his son was born. Years later he comes back to his home city as a teacher, in a robe, with a bowl. The boy's mother points to the monk and says: that's your father.
Go and ask him for your inheritance. So Rahula walks up to the Buddha, and asks.

teach.b: In the Vinaya, the Buddha's answer is to have the boy ordained. His inheritance is the teaching itself. Then the Buddha's own father, King Suddhodana, comes to him in pain.
When you left, it hurt. When your brother left, it hurt. Now Rahula.
Love for a son, he says, cuts through the skin, the flesh, the bone, to the marrow. Let no child be ordained without the parents' consent. And the Buddha makes it a rule.
So two views live side by side. One says the best gift a parent can give is the path itself, and the Buddha gave it.

teach.h: A GRANDFATHER'S GRIEF BECOMES A RULE.
teach.b: The other keeps the grandfather's grief in the record, and in the rule book.
Both are in the same text. Neither side gets erased: the tradition remembers the gift and the cost in the same breath. Then a sutta shows the father teaching his son himself, with a mirror.
What's a mirror for, Rahula? For looking at yourself.
So look before you act, while you act, and after: does this harm you, or anyone else? If it does, stop; if it's done, tell someone you trust, and do better.
That's Buddhist reflection, taught by a father to a child, and it isn't one big talk.

how: The Vinaya's ordination questions ask whether a candidate has the parents' permission, a rule it traces to King Suddhodana's grief. Some Buddhist teachers use the Buddha's advice to Rahula, looking at each act before, during and after, as a daily practice of reflection.

o: raising a child as a daily practice of care
a vow some parents take before a birth
a strict schedule that makes kids behave well

games.q: the Buddha's son: tap the pairs.
p: go and ask him for your inheritance
received the teaching as his inheritance
love for a son cuts to the marrow
look before, during and after you act

s: the Buddha never saw his son again after leaving home
he returned to his home city; Rahula was ordained, and a sutta shows the Buddha teaching him.
after the king's plea, the Buddha ruled that no child be ordained without the parents' consent
the Vinaya ties the rule to Suddhodana's grief.
the Buddha's mirror lesson is about checking how you look
it's about looking at your acts, before, during and after: does this harm anyone?

games.q: a friend says: "the Buddha walked out on his kid. end of story." what's the strongest case for the other side, from the texts?
o: he came back, gave his son the teaching, and made a rule from his father's grief.
his son didn't mind at all, so there's really nothing to argue about.
monks don't have families, so the question doesn't apply to him.
games.why: the Vinaya keeps both: Rahula ordained as his inheritance, and Suddhodana's grief turned into the consent rule. Then the mirror sutta: the father teaching his son himself.

practice: Bring to mind a parent, or someone who parented you. Send them a short thank-you text for one ordinary thing they did over and over, or, if they're gone, say it to them quietly.
Then sit with your hands open for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Parenting as practice: the daily mirror the Buddha gave his son, and the rule his father's grief wrote. Look before, during and after, and mend what harms.

orig.note: Pali: mirror. The Buddha asks Rahula what a mirror is for: for looking at yourself.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: every day a practice, the mirror held before, during and after each thing you do. Day 1683, done.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga 1.54 (at Kapilavatthu, Rahula's mother sends him to ask for his inheritance; Sariputta ordains him; Suddhodana's grief, love for a son cutting to the marrow; the rule that no son be ordained without the parents' consent)
Majjhima Nikaya 61, Ambalatthika-Rahulovada Sutta (what is a mirror for? for reflection; reflect before, during and after every act of body, speech and mind)
